hero.title: Business Cards & Spend Management Index
hero.subtitle: How six platforms explain spending controls, rewards and cross-border business payments.
hero.scope: This Index examines how six platforms explain business cards, spend management and cross-border payments to Canadian businesses. It uses dated public sources and evaluates communication and enquiry journeys. It does not test product performance, assess regulatory compliance or recommend a provider for your business.
hero.draft_note: Draft for editorial review. This edition is not published.

findings.dek: Three things a Canadian business reading these sites would run into, each linked to the wording behind it. They describe how the offers are explained, not how the products perform.

items.question: Is the advertised reward what I would earn?
items.title: Reward rates and their conditions were often stated in different places
items.body: Five of the six platforms published a reward rate. At two (Venn and Loop), visible statements on different pages did not agree for some plans: Venn's cards page says its cashback has no caps while its pricing footnote caps it on two plans, and Loop's cards page says rewards come on all spend while its Basic plan earns only on CAD spend. Airwallex's visible pages say 1%, with a 2% figure only in the page title shown in search results and link previews. Float and Keep publish their conditions on the pricing page.
items.denominator: 5 platforms that published a reward rate. Ramp publishes Canadian rewards terms but no rate.

items.question: Does "no FX fee" mean I never pay to convert?
items.title: Every "no FX fee" claim described one kind of transaction
items.body: All six platforms published a statement of no FX fee, no FX markup or a 0% FX fee. Each covered a specific case, such as spending from a balance in the same currency, four approved currencies or a USD card, and each site or its terms describes a fee, rate or margin for other conversions: for example a 1.00% automatic conversion fee at Airwallex and a margin of up to 3% in Ramp's Canadian card terms. Keep's pricing page lists an FX fee of 0% for banking, while its card agreement sets a 3% card conversion fee.
items.denominator: 6 of 6 platforms; card spending, FX conversion and transfers were checked separately for each.

items.question: What kind of card is this, really?
items.title: Four cards share one issuer, but the way you fund them differs
items.body: Peoples Trust Company issues the Venn, Ramp, Keep and Airwallex cards. Behind that shared issuer the models differ: Venn's card spends money already in the account, Keep's is a charge card paid in full, Ramp's Canadian terms require each statement to be paid in full by pre-authorised debit, Airwallex's terms say its card spends the wallet balance and is not a credit card while its pricing also lists a credit line, Float offers both a pre-funded card and short-term credit, and Loop's purchases draw on a credit facility.
items.denominator: 6 platforms; for Airwallex, the terms for the listed credit line were not found.

findings.take: When a headline offer and its condition live on different pages, the reader has to put them back together. Ask your team to list every place your main offer appears (ads, landing pages, pricing, terms) and check that the condition travels with the rate each time.

examples.dek: Four observed examples of how an offer, proof or next step was explained. They are examples to learn from, not winning platforms.

items.title: A savings figure labelled as the provider's own estimate
items.body: The Bells of Steel case study presents $10,000 a year in savings and says in the text that Loop calculated it. The same site's homepage averages ($40,000 and 12 hours a year) carry no basis I could find, so the labelled figure stands out.
items.lesson: A reader can weigh a number when they know who calculated it and how.

items.title: "Up to" with the threshold in a numbered footnote
items.body: Float's pages say "Up to 1% cashback". The pricing page footnote gives the condition: 1% applies above $25k of monthly spending per card program. The rate below that threshold was not on the pages I reviewed.
items.lesson: "Up to" signals a condition; the footnote states it, but only on the pricing page.

items.title: Eligibility stated on the card page
items.body: Ramp's Canadian card page lists what a business needs: a Canadian, US or UK-registered entity, a Business Number and a linked Canadian bank account, underwritten on the business with no personal guarantee. The sign-up screen itself asks for one email and does not repeat the list.
items.lesson: A reader can check whether they qualify before giving an email, if they read the card page first.

items.title: A competitor named inside a customer story
items.body: Airwallex's Adaria Vending Services story, about a Canadian company expanding into the US, names Venn and Wise as tools the company used before. The outcomes it reports are qualitative, such as cards issued in under 24 hours.
items.lesson: Naming the prior setup makes the switch concrete; the outcome is still the provider's account of its customer.

venn.positioning: Canadian business banking with accounts, cards and transfers in one place, for businesses outside Quebec.
venn.offer: 1% cashback, no FX fee from matching-currency balances, and plans from $0. The cards page says the cashback has no caps; the pricing footnote caps it on Essentials and Plus.
venn.explanation: The funding model is clear in the agreement (funds must be in the account first). The FX fee by plan is on pricing and in the agreement, separate from the no-FX-fee line on the cards page. The number of currencies you can send is given as 36 on two pages and 33 in a help article.
venn.proof: The visible homepage counts agree at 15,000+ (a 4,000+ figure is in the page code but set not to display). The Flow case study reports time saved without figures. The transfers page claims FX rates up to 2.75% cheaper than banks, with no basis I could find.
venn.journey: "Open a free account" leads to a sign-up screen asking for email, password and password confirmation (or Google or Microsoft sign-in). It says "No personal credit check or guarantee" and "Get started in 5 minutes". The next step creates an account, so I stopped there.
venn.observation: The cashback statement on the cards page and the footnote on pricing cannot both be read literally for Essentials and Plus customers.
missing: Steps after account creation (needs an account)
venn.take: Your cards page and your pricing page are read as one offer. Ask your team whether a visitor who sees only your highest-traffic page would come away with the right picture of caps and plan limits.

float.positioning: Corporate cards and spend software for Canadian companies, with a pre-funded card for any business and short-term credit for those that qualify.
float.offer: Up to 1% cashback, 0.25% FX, USD cards without foreign transaction fees, account interest of 2.5% (up to 3.5% in a promotion) and credit up to $3M+ subject to eligibility.
float.explanation: The two card models are named and separated, and the cards page names both cards behind its Visa or Mastercard line: a CAD Visa card and a USD Mastercard. The cashback threshold is a pricing footnote. An image badge says "Up to 3.5% interest"; the condition, a 12-month promotion on new balances above a baseline, is in the legal terms.
float.proof: The Impact Kitchen story reports more than 100 hours a year saved. "Save up to 90% on FX" carries no basis I could find.
float.journey: "See a demo" leads to a Book a Demo form with eight required fields, including monthly card spend and product interest. The consent line says submitting lets Float contact you; nothing says what happens after booking. The homepage email box is a separate start route.
float.observation: Both "up to" figures, cashback and interest, lead with the best case; the condition for each is on another page (a pricing footnote and the promotion terms).
missing: What happens after a demo is booked
float.take: An "up to" figure invites the question "up to, if what?". A practical test: put the condition for each "up to" figure on the same screen as the figure, and measure qualified demo requests against questions about rates.

ramp.positioning: A spend platform with Canadian cards, eligibility for Canadian, US or UK-registered entities, and global proof.
ramp.offer: Free and Plus plans, CAD and USD cards, and CAD or USD spend without the FX markup.
ramp.explanation: Eligibility is stated clearly on the cards page. The Canadian card terms say statements are paid in full by pre-authorised debit and cap the conversion margin at 3% for other currencies. The Canadian rewards terms exclude non-CAD purchases and give no rate. I found no Canadian multi-currency account or transfer fees on the Canadian pages.
ramp.proof: 85,000 customers worldwide, a receipt figure labelled as internal data, and quotes from large brands. None of the proof is specific to Canada.
ramp.journey: "Get started" leads to a Canadian sign-up screen with one email field and "Continue application"; the eligibility list is not repeated there. The header "See a demo" link goes to a page outside the Canadian site.
ramp.observation: The footer names Ramp Business Corporation as the registered payment service provider, while the Canadian card terms name Ramp Business Canada Corporation; both appear on the Bank of Canada registry.
missing: Steps after the email (needs an application)
ramp.take: When a regional page borrows global proof and links, the buyer has to work out which parts apply to them. Ask your team to mark every claim on your regional page as local or global, and test labelling global figures as such.

loop.positioning: Cross-border finance for Canadian businesses, presented as "Canada's first no-FX credit card" with global accounts and payments.
loop.offer: No FX fee in four currencies, points on card spend, free payments for now, and credit up to $1M.
loop.explanation: The four-currency limit and the 1.5% fee outside it are in the card agreement; the pricing page states the four currencies. The cards page says rewards come on all spend with no tiers; on the Basic plan, only CAD spend earns points. The pricing page opens on yearly prices ($71 and $250 a month billed annually).
loop.proof: The Bells of Steel case study labels its $10,000 saving as Loop's calculation. The homepage averages ($40,000 and 12 hours) and the "first" claim carry no basis I could find.
loop.journey: "Open Account" leads to a sign-up form (name, legal business name, email, mobile phone) with a panel listing the two steps that follow: business information, including the CRA ID, and identity, with date of birth and government ID. "See a Demo" opens an interactive product tour.
loop.observation: The same site shows both a labelled estimate and unlabelled averages, which makes the difference easy to see.
missing: Steps after the first form (needs a submission)
loop.take: Where your proof states its basis, a buyer can weigh it; where it does not, they have to trust it. Ask your team which three figures on your homepage could be challenged, and add the source line to each.

keep.positioning: An all-in-one corporate card and banking product for Canadian companies, called "Canada's #1" in the page title.
keep.offer: Points with up to 56 fee-free days, multi-currency accounts in five currencies, and 90-day trials on plans from $79 a month.
keep.explanation: Reward rates depend on plan, and the plan table shows them; the card page comparison gives the top-tier rates without naming the plan. The card agreement sets a 3% card conversion fee that I did not find on the card, pricing or FAQ pages, and the card page comparison row for FX fees shows reward rates in Keep's column.
keep.proof: "Trusted by 5,000+ Canadian Companies" and "Canada's #1", with no basis for the ranking on the pages I reviewed. No case study was found. Keep's pages did not show a registration number, though both registries list Keep Technologies Corp.
keep.journey: Every start button found leads to one sign-up route, which showed "We're not accepting new applications at this time" and offered log-in to existing customers. The message names no product.
keep.observation: The marketing pages still present the offer, start buttons and "Applications do not impact your credit score", while the one sign-up route they lead to says applications are closed.
missing: Whether the closed sign-up route affects every Keep product
keep.take: If a journey is paused, the pages that send people to it are the first thing they see. Ask your team what a visitor who clicks your main button today actually reaches, and whether the page they leave from says so.

airwallex.positioning: A global financial platform for Canadian businesses expanding abroad: accounts in 20+ currencies, transfers and multi-currency cards.
airwallex.offer: 1% cashback on card spend, no foreign transaction fee from a held currency, transfers with $0 fees on local rails, and plans from $0.
airwallex.explanation: Pricing states FX at 0.5% above interbank for major currencies and SWIFT fees. The no-fee card line covers spending from a currency you hold; when the wallet does not hold it, the card terms add an automatic conversion fee, listed at 1.00% in the fee schedule. The visible pages say 1% cashback; the pricing page says up to 1% on local CAD spend, and the rebate terms were not found.
airwallex.proof: The homepage gives 200,000 and 600,000+ businesses; the 600,000 figure says it includes customers served through platforms. The Adaria story is Canadian and reports qualitative outcomes.
airwallex.journey: "Get started" leads to one business email field; continuing agrees to receive marketing communications. The demo form was not opened.
airwallex.observation: The page title promises 2% cashback while every visible statement says 1%, and the title is what search results and shared links show.
airwallex.take: The page title is often the first thing a buyer reads, in a search result or a shared link. Ask your team whether every title and preview on your site states the same offer as the page it leads to.

patterns.dek: Patterns that hold across the group, with the platforms that support them and the exceptions. None shows cause and effect.

items.title: Figures often appeared without their basis
items.body: Every platform published a customer count or savings figure. Savings and ranking claims without a stated basis appeared at Venn (FX up to 2.75% cheaper than banks), Float (save up to 90% on FX), Loop (average savings) and Keep ("Canada's #1").
items.exceptions: Loop's case study labels its estimate; Ramp labels its receipt figure as internal data; Airwallex says its 600,000 figure includes customers served through platforms.
items.denominator: 6 of 6 published such a figure; 4 of 6 gave at least one without a basis I could find.

items.title: The first screen rarely said what happens next
items.body: Venn asks for an email and password to create an account, Ramp and Airwallex for a single email, and Float for an eight-field demo form; none of these first screens says what happens after you continue. Keep's start buttons led to a closed-applications page.
items.exceptions: Loop's sign-up lists the two steps that follow and what they need (CRA ID, date of birth, government ID).
items.denominator: 6 of 6 first screens observed in a browser on 23 October 2026; none followed past the first screen.

items.title: Registry entries matched the providers' own statements, with two gaps in the wording
items.body: All six legal entities are registered with FINTRAC as money services businesses. Five appear on the Bank of Canada registry of payment service providers; Airwallex (Canada) International Payments Limited is on its list of applicants, as Airwallex's own footer says. Keep's pages did not show a registration number, and Ramp's footer names a different Ramp entity from its Canadian card terms. These are registry entries, not an endorsement, a licence or a safety rating.
items.denominator: 6 of 6 checked in both registries on 23 October 2026, 12:13 p.m. to 12:14 p.m. Toronto time.

patterns.take: Buyers of financial products look for the basis behind a number and for what happens after they click. Ask your team which figure on your site a careful buyer would question first, and what your first form says about the next step.

tests.dek: Three tests a marketing team could run on its own pages, each tied to a finding above. They are proposals to discuss, not results, and none needs a provider's internal data.

items.title: Put the reward condition beside the rate
items.example: Venn's cards page says 1% with no caps while its pricing footnote caps it on two plans; Loop's cards page says rewards on all spend while its Basic plan earns only on CAD spend.
items.uncertainty: Will I earn the advertised rate on my plan and at my spend level?
items.change: Show the cap, threshold or plan condition in the same block as the headline rate on the card page. Keep the rate, the design, the button and the terms the same.
items.measure: Qualified applications or demo requests (meeting your eligibility rules) per visitor to the card page.
items.guardrail: Rewards questions to sales and support in the first 30 days after sign-up, and plan mix.
items.comparison: A randomised split of card-page traffic with the same sources, the same attribution window and the same definition of a qualified application. Count button clicks separately from qualified applications.
items.limitation: If rewards are not a main reason buyers choose you, or traffic is too small to separate the two versions, the result will be inconclusive. Legal review of the wording comes first.

items.title: Say which transactions a "no FX fee" claim covers
items.example: All six platforms' no-fee statements covered specific cases (a matching balance, four currencies, a USD card), with other conversions priced elsewhere.
items.uncertainty: Will I pay to convert when I buy in a currency I do not hold?
items.change: Replace a general "no FX fees" line with one that names the case, followed by one line saying what applies otherwise. Keep the page layout, offer and button the same.
items.measure: Completed applications from the FX or cards page.
items.guardrail: FX-related support questions and disputed charges in the first 60 days after sign-up.
items.comparison: A randomised split with the same audiences and attribution window; if traffic is low, run the versions in matched consecutive periods and record the dates.
items.limitation: Required disclosures stay in place; this changes the summary, not the terms. Seasonal travel or trade cycles can swamp the difference.

items.title: State eligibility and the next step before the form
items.example: Ramp lists entity, Business Number and bank account requirements on its card page, and Loop's sign-up lists the two steps ahead and the documents they need; the other first screens asked for an email or account details without saying what follows.
items.uncertainty: Do I qualify, and what happens after I give my email?
items.change: Add a short "Before you start" list above the first form field: who can apply, what you need, which provinces are served, and what happens after submitting. Keep the form fields and verification steps the same.
items.measure: The share of form starts that become qualified applications.
items.guardrail: Total form starts and completed submissions from eligible businesses, so the list does not turn away people who qualify.
items.comparison: A randomised split with consistent audiences; report clicks, form starts, submissions and qualified applications as separate numbers.
items.limitation: If eligibility rules change during the test, or most traffic is already qualified, the result will not separate the two versions. Never remove necessary identity or eligibility checks.

method.selection: The founder selected these six platforms as a comparison set of providers that market business cards and spend management to Canadian businesses. They are not presented as the largest, the most used or the best, and other providers exist.
method.dates: Public pages were fetched by a server on 23 October 2026 from 10:39 a.m. to 10:48 a.m. Toronto time, a browser pass checked them from 12:00 p.m. to 12:14 p.m., and one more legal page (the Airwallex fee schedule) was fetched at 2:10 p.m. Every observation carries its own capture time.
method.public_only: I read only public pages: no accounts, logins, forms submitted, credit checks or transactions. A server fetch does not run JavaScript, so a browser pass then checked what visitors see, followed each enquiry journey to its first screen and looked up the FINTRAC and Bank of Canada registries. Where the two differed, the page reports what a visitor sees and keeps the server reading in the evidence.
statuses: An applicable official source states it. This does not mean it was tested.
The pages I reviewed did not establish it. It may exist elsewhere.
Relevant sources differ and the difference is unresolved.
An applicable source says it is not available.
limitations: Pages change. Every observation is dated to its capture and may no longer be current.
The browser pass used a normal Chrome profile that was not signed in to any of the six providers. Journeys were followed only to the first screen; nothing was submitted.
US and global pages were not used as Canadian facts. Where a Canadian page carried US disclosures, that is recorded as an observation about the page.
Registry entries were checked on 23 October 2026 and are recorded as displayed. They are not a compliance assessment, an endorsement or a safety rating.
This edition does not compare FX costs or product performance and does not recommend a provider.
method.corrections: If an observation is wrong or out of date, email Hello@helpmemarketing.com with the page and the correction. Confirmed corrections will be made with a dated note.

help.heading: If you market a financial product
help.body: I can read your own pages the way this Index reads these six: how the offer, its conditions, the proof and the next step come across to a buyer. This is a free review of your marketing by Help Me Marketing. It is not a card application, and it is not financial, legal or regulatory advice.
